10 cherry tomatoes: Drain the beans and rinse with cold water.
Drain the tuna and break it into large flakes with a fork.
Slice the onion thinly, rub it with salt and rinse.
Halve the tomatoes and chop the parsley.
Whisk the olive oil, lemon juice and salt to make a dressing.
Gently toss all the ingredients with the dressing in a bowl.
Count tuna as part of your weekly fish intake; in pregnancy, don’t exceed 1–2 portions a week.
Making it the night before lets the flavours develop, but add the tomatoes just before serving.
Broad bean purée (fava)
1.5 cups dried split broad beans
Wash the beans several times, soak overnight and drain.
Chop the onion roughly.
Put the beans, onion, 2 tablespoons olive oil and the water in a pan and bring to the boil; skim off the foam.
Cook over low heat for 40–45 minutes, stirring now and then, until the beans have completely broken down.
Add the sugar, salt and lemon juice and blend.
Pour into a wetted dish and level; once cool, chill in the fridge for at least 2 hours.
Turn out and slice; garnish with olive oil and chopped dill.
The purée thickens as it rests; it’s normal for it to look a little runny while hot.
People with favism (G6PD deficiency) must not eat broad beans.
Baked salmon quinoa bowl
2 salmon fillets (about 300 g)
Rinse the quinoa in a fine sieve, bring to the boil with the water and cook covered for 15 minutes, then let it rest.
Place the salmon on a tray lined with baking paper and drizzle with olive oil and half the lemon.
Bake for 12–15 minutes, until the flesh flakes easily and is opaque in the centre.
Slice the avocado and cucumber, grate the carrot.
Arrange the quinoa, rocket and vegetables in bowls and place the salmon on top.
Drizzle with the rest of the lemon juice and sprinkle with sesame.
In pregnancy, salmon must be fully cooked.
You can use baked chicken breast instead of salmon.
Keep the salmon and quinoa in separate containers in the fridge for 1 day.
Grilled chicken bulgur salad
Soak the bulgur in hot water, cover and leave for 15 minutes.
Slice the chicken thinly and toss with 1 tablespoon olive oil and thyme.
Cook the chicken in a grill pan for 5–6 minutes on each side, until completely white inside.
Finely chop the tomatoes, cucumber, parsley and mint.
Add the remaining olive oil, lemon juice and salt and mix; slice the chicken and arrange on top.
The chicken must not stay pink inside.
You can use quinoa instead of bulgur.
Serve for lunch or as a light dinner.
Courgette spaghetti with tomato sauce
3 medium courgettes
5–6 basil leaves
Cut the courgettes into thin ribbons with a spiraliser or peeler.
Grate the tomatoes and finely chop the garlic.
Heat the olive oil in a pan and stir the garlic for 30 seconds.
Add the tomatoes and salt and cook for 6–7 minutes until the sauce thickens.
Add the courgette ribbons and toss for 2 minutes, keeping them crisp.
Tear in the basil and serve with the cheese.
Overcooked courgette releases water and turns mushy.
For a more filling dish, add boiled chickpeas.
Lentil and cauliflower bowl
Wash the lentils and boil them in the water for 20–25 minutes so they keep their bite; drain.
Break the cauliflower into florets and toss with olive oil, turmeric, cumin and salt.
Spread in a single layer on a tray and roast for 25–30 minutes, until golden at the edges.
Arrange the rocket, lentils and cauliflower in bowls.
Add yoghurt on top and serve.
If you don’t crowd the tray, the cauliflower roasts instead of steaming.
A meal rich in fibre and plant protein.
Baked falafel
1.5 cups dried chickpeas (soaked overnight)
1 dessertspoon ground coriander
Preheat the oven to 200°C, line a tray with baking paper and brush with 1 tablespoon olive oil.
Drain the soaked chickpeas and dry them well.
Pulse the chickpeas, onion, garlic and parsley in a food processor until they look like coarse sand.
